title: Forgiving the gunman (1983)
hookLine: John Paul II visits in prison the man who shot him

lines: A CELL IN ROME, TWO CHAIRS.
THEY TALK FOR A LONG TIME.
cards: Cameras catch the scene, but not the words. Two chairs pulled close in a small prison cell in Rome. One man in white, one in a prisoner's clothes.
They lean in until their heads nearly touch, and they talk quietly for a long time. At one point the man in white holds the other man's hand. The prisoner is Mehmet Ali Ağca.
Some time before, in Saint Peter's Square, in front of a crowd, he raised a pistol and shot the man now sitting beside him. The visitor is John Paul the Second.

teach.b: Four moments make this story. First, the square. John Paul was riding slowly through the crowd in an open car when shots rang out.

teach.h: FROM A HOSPITAL BED: MY BROTHER.
teach.b: He was badly wounded and rushed to a hospital, and for a time it wasn't clear he would live. The gunman was caught on the spot. Second, the hospital.
Within days, still weak, the pope spoke to the world by radio from his bed. He asked people to pray for the brother who had shot him, whom he had sincerely forgiven. Not the gunman.
Third, the cell. After his recovery he went to the prison himself. No letter, no bishop in his place.

He sat down and talked with the man, and afterward said that what they talked about would remain a secret between them, and that he had spoken to him as a brother whom he had pardoned and who had his complete trust.
In Matthew's Gospel, Jesus names prison visits among the things done for him, in the Douay-Rheims: "I was in prison, and you came to me." Fourth, what forgiveness didn't do.
Ağca stayed in prison for years after the visit. The pope didn't pretend the shooting was small or that justice didn't matter.
Catholic teaching holds forgiveness and justice side by side: you can release a debt in your heart and still let the courts do their work.

teach.h: I WAS IN PRISON, AND YOU CAME TO ME.
teach.b: Two chairs, two men, a held hand, and words they kept between them.

how: Catholics who volunteer in prison ministry visit inmates, often bringing Communion and listening, and some point to John Paul II's visit to Ağca and to Jesus's words in Matthew 25 as their pattern.

games.q: you're the pope, recovered from a gunshot wound. the man who shot you sits in a Roman prison. what do you do?
o: send a bishop with a letter.
go to the cell yourself and sit with him.
leave it to the courts and say nothing.
games.why: he went himself, sat close, held his hand, and talked with him privately.

practice: Let someone come to mind who hurt you, not the deepest wound, something you can hold today, and picture them in a chair close to yours.

You don't have to say it's fine: you can name what happened, and if you're ready, say I forgive you; if you're not, leave the chair there for another day. Forgiving never means putting yourself in harm's way.
If you pray, you can pray for them by name, as the pope did.

wordCard.voice: Forgiving the gunman. John Paul the Second, shot in Saint Peter's Square, forgave Mehmet Ali Ağca and went to visit him in prison.

carryVoice: Your line: he went to the cell. Forgiveness walked in, and justice stayed. Day nine hundred twenty-five, complete.
